My name is Robyn Elston, I'm the National Manager of Local Government at NZTA
Waka Kotahi, and we appreciate the opportunity to appear
before the committee regarding the petition of Free Fares New Zealand, stop the
proposed public transport fare hikes.
I'd like to start by directly addressing the central concern
raised in the petition. NZTA recognizes that fare increases
can affect affordability and can be challenging for some public transport
users, particularly during a period of ongoing cost of living pressures.
We also recognize the important role public transport plays in supporting access to
work, education, healthcare, and community participation,
as well as its contribution to reducing congestion and supporting environmental
outcomes.
However, public transport services must also be financially
sustainable. Over recent years, the proportion of public transport
operating costs funded through private revenue has fallen significantly.
National private share was approximately 33% in
2018/2019, and had declined to
private share declined, a greater proportion of operating costs was funded by
taxpayers and ratepayers. In response to GPS and Land
Transport 24 setting the expectation that public transport authorities
work towards increasing private share over time, and NZTA's
role is to implement that direction.
It is important to be clear about what NZTA does and does not do.
NZTA does not set public transport fares, determine concession
policies, or decide local service levels.
Except for SuperGold and Community Connect, which are set by the government, the
remaining transport fares concession policy decisions remain the
responsibility of public transport authorities and their elected
representatives. NZTA has not directed councils to
implement specific fare increases.
Our role has been to work alongside public transport authorities to establish
appropriate targets and support them in identifying how those targets can
be achieved.
When developing those targets, NZTA engaged extensively
with public transport authorities across the country.
Following that engagement, the final targets were approved by the NZTA board,
and they were lower than those that were originally proposed and were tailored to
regional circumstances.
NZTA also encouraged authorities to consider approaches that avoided
adverse outcomes, such as significant patronage
decline.
Ultimately, we do not see this as a choice between affordable public transport and
sustainable public transport.
The challenge is finding the right balance between affordability, patronage growth,
environmental objectives, and long-term funding sustainability.
And NZTA's role is to support that balance while implementing the expectations set
by government through GPS '24. Thank you.
